title: Writing a brief nobody has to clarify
desc: One sentence that fills What, When, Uses and Sends to correctly, and what to correct on the card before you start.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can write the one sentence for a Cowork task so that the card's four lines come out right, and correct the lines that did not before you press Set up and test.

steps.title: Nobody is there to answer
steps.bodyMd:
At 07:30 tomorrow a run starts, and nobody is awake to answer a question about it.

Bart does procurement at Van Dijk Groep, a Dutch building-supplies firm. His first sentence reads: **"Keep an eye on the supplier mail."**

Cowork does not come back to ask *which* mailbox, *when*, or what *"an eye"* means. It works with what the sentence says. When the AI works a task out on a run, it is even told outright: do not ask follow-up questions, this runs unattended.

In chat a vague prompt costs you one follow-up message. In Cowork it costs you the whole run, and you find out the next morning. The good news: before anything exists, Cowork shows you what it understood, so you can catch it on the card.

steps.title: One sentence, four answers
steps.bodyMd:
The card asks four questions of every sentence. Write the answers in, and nothing is left to guess.

1. **What**: the work that comes out. A digest, a list, a draft, a table, with the detail that makes it useful: which fields, how many, what to leave out.
2. **When**: a day and a time, or how often.
3. **Uses**: the apps to read from, by their name.
4. **Sends to**: who gets it. Yourself, and anyone else by e-mail address.

Bart's second attempt:

> *Every weekday at 07:30, summarise the new supplier mail in Outlook per supplier, with the order number, the amount and the reply deadline, and send it to me and inkoop@vandijk.nl.*

Same job. Every line of the card has its answer.

steps.title: Which line will come out wrong?
steps.instruction: Four sentences Bart nearly sent. Each one leaves one of the four lines to chance. Match the sentence to what the card will show.

pairs.left: "Summarise the new supplier mail in Outlook with order number, amount and deadline, and send it to me."
pairs.right: When: the card asks Which day?
pairs.note: No day or time at all. The card says your sentence does not say when, and the start button stays off until you pick a day.

pairs.left: "Every Monday at 08:00, list last week's late deliveries per supplier and send it to me."
pairs.right: Uses: Cowork picks the apps itself
pairs.note: No app is named, so none is pre-selected. Cowork picks the apps while it sets up the steps, and you see them before anything runs. Name the app if you already know it.

pairs.left: "Every Friday at 16:00, list this week's open quotes from Outlook and send it to the purchasing team."
pairs.note: "The purchasing team" is not an address. Only e-mail addresses written in the sentence reach Sends to; add the team's address, or type it on the card.

pairs.left: "Every weekday at 07:30, keep an eye on Outlook and send it to me."
pairs.note: A topic is not a deliverable. Say digest, list, table or draft, with its fields, or the steps guess what to make, differently every time.

steps.title: How Cowork reads each line
steps.bodyMd:
- **What** on the card is the task's **name**, at most 60 characters, so the list stays scannable. What the task should do is kept beside it, and you find it again on the task under Settings → What.
- **When**: vague times become fixed hours. *Morning* is 08:00, *midday* 12:00, *afternoon* 14:00, *evening* 18:00, *night* 21:00.
- **Uses**: only apps your sentence names by their name are pre-selected. Name none, and the card says Cowork picks the apps it needs while it sets up the steps.
- **Sends to**: **Me** is always there to start with, plus every e-mail address written in the sentence. *"Send it to me and sam@…"* shows both.

Reading the sentence creates nothing. Nothing reaches **Your tasks** until you press **Set up and test**.

steps.question: Bart writes "…and send it to purchasing". On the card, Sends to shows only Me. What should he do?

choices.label: Add purchasing's e-mail address on the card (or write it in the sentence) before he presses Set up and test.
Nothing: at 07:30 the run will work out who purchasing is and send it there.
choices.feedback: The run is told exactly who to send to, and that is what Sends to shows. A name of a team is not an address, so nobody in purchasing would get it.

choices.label: Start it now and add the address later on the task page.
choices.feedback: On the task page, Sends to only shows who receives it; to send it to someone else you say so in the sentence under What, and that rebuilds and retests the steps. The card is the easy place.

steps.explanation: Only written e-mail addresses become recipients. The card has an address field with Add for exactly this, and a chip with × to take one off.

steps.title: Try a sentence here
steps.body: Type a sentence with all four answers in it and choose Show what I understood. The card appears right under this box. Nothing is created until you press Set up and test, so Cancel is always safe.

steps.title: What you can correct on the card
steps.bodyMd:
Every line of **This is what I understood** can be changed before the task exists:

- **What**: type a better name in the field.
- **When**: **Change** opens **Which day?** with *Just once, today*, *Every day*, weekdays or one weekday, and the time beside it.
- **Uses**: take an app off with its ×, or pick one under **Add an app**.
- **Sends to**: take **Me** or an address off, add an address with **Add**.

And you can still edit the sentence itself. The card reads it again (*Reading your sentence again…*) and follows the new words, except on the lines you changed by hand: those stay as you set them.

steps.question: Bart changed When on the card to every weekday at 07:30. Then he adds "…and flag anything due within two days" to the sentence, which still says "every day". What does When show after the card reads it again?

choices.label: Still every weekday at 07:30: a line he changed by hand keeps his choice, the other lines follow the new sentence.
Every day, because the sentence was read again from the start.
choices.feedback: Reading again only replaces the lines he did not touch. What he set by hand on the card is kept.

choices.label: The card closes and he has to start over.
choices.feedback: Editing the sentence never throws the card away. Only emptying the box, or Cancel, closes it.

steps.explanation: Fix the sentence for the work, fix the card for the details. A line you change by hand wins over what the sentence says.

steps.title: When it sends to someone else
steps.bodyMd:
As soon as Sends to holds anyone besides you, the card shows a checkbox **Show me each message first**, ticked. With it, *nothing goes to someone else before you have seen it, under Needs you*: a card shows the message with **Send** and **Don’t send**.

Unticking it does not make the task send on its own right away. The card says so: *Cowork still shows you each message at first. After 10 runs you let through, you can choose “Don’t ask” in the task.*

That choice lives on the task afterwards, under **Settings → Sends to → Ask me**, and it applies to tasks with fixed steps.

steps.question: Saskia's monthly report goes to her and to the HR manager. She unticks Show me each message first, because she trusts it. On the first run, what happens to the message for the HR manager?

choices.label: It still waits for her under Needs you; Don't ask only opens on the task after 10 runs she let through.
It goes straight to the HR manager, because she unticked the box.
choices.feedback: That is what the box looks like it does, but the card itself says otherwise: Cowork still shows each message at first, and Don't ask is only offered after 10 runs let through.

choices.label: It is never sent, because a task may only send to its owner.
choices.feedback: A task may send to the addresses under Sends to. The question is only whether she sees the message first, and at the start she does.

steps.explanation: Trust is earned run by run. At first every message to someone else waits for one tap; once enough runs went through without a stop, the task offers to let them go.

steps.title: Your turn: the sentence for the thing you redo every week
steps.instruction: Think of the job you retype most often: the Monday list, the weekly summary, the check you keep forgetting. Write it as ONE sentence for Cowork that answers all four lines: what comes out (with the fields or length that make it useful), when, which app it reads from by name, and who it goes to (yourself, and any colleague by e-mail address). Then add one short line: which line of the card you would check first, and why.
steps.placeholder: e.g. Every Friday at 15:00, list this week's closed support tickets from Zendesk with the three most common problems and one example each, and send it to me and lead@example.com. I would check Sends to first, because…

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Write one sentence with four answers**: what comes out, when, which app by name, and who gets it by address. No question left in it for someone who will not be there.
- **Read the card before you start**: Which day? means you did not say when; no app chips means Cowork will pick them; only Me under Sends to means no address was written.
- **Correct on the card, not afterwards**: a line you change by hand keeps your choice, and every message to someone else waits for you at first.

Next chapter you make one for real, approve its steps, run it, and read a failure on purpose.

ex-cowork-brief.title: Write the sentence for a Cowork task
ex-cowork-brief.task: Write one sentence for a Cowork task that answers the four lines of the confirmation card: what comes out (with the detail that makes it useful), when it runs, which app it reads from by name, and who receives it (the learner, and anyone else by e-mail address). Then add one line saying which line of the card they would check first and why.
criteria: States a concrete result (a digest, list, draft, table) with the detail that makes it useful, not just a topic to watch.
Says when it runs: a day and a time, a repeat, or explicitly once today.
Names the app or source it reads from by name (a mailbox app, a calendar, meeting notes, a ticket system).
Says who receives it, with any colleague given as an e-mail address rather than a team name, and adds a sensible line about which card line to check first.
ex-cowork-brief.guidance: Reward sentences that would fill the card correctly with nobody available to clarify. Score below pass: a topic with no result ("keep an eye on our competitors"), no timing at all, a recipient given only as a team or role ("send it to purchasing") with no address, or a sentence that asks the reader a question. A sentence that only sends to the learner is fine. Naming what to do when there is nothing to report is a plus, not a requirement.

practiceTopic.title: Writing the sentence for a Cowork task
practiceTopic.summary: How one sentence becomes the card's What, When, Uses and Sends to, what each line needs to come out right, and what can be corrected on the card.
facts: The confirmation card 'This is what I understood' has four lines: What (the task's name, at most 60 characters), When, Uses and Sends to.
When the sentence does not say when, the card asks 'Which day?' and the start button stays off until a day is picked; the choices include 'Just once, today', every day, weekdays and one weekday.
Vague times map to fixed hours: morning is 08:00, midday 12:00, afternoon 14:00, evening 18:00 and night 21:00.
Uses pre-selects only the apps the sentence names by name; with none named the card says Cowork picks the apps it needs while it sets up the steps.
Sends to starts with Me and adds every e-mail address written in the sentence; a team name is not an address.
Editing the sentence makes the card read it again ('Reading your sentence again…'); lines changed by hand on the card keep their value.

When someone besides the owner is under Sends to, 'Show me each message first' is ticked; unticked, Cowork still shows each message at first, and 'Don't ask' is offered on the task only after 10 runs let through.
When the AI works a task out on a run it is told not to ask follow-up questions, because the run is unattended.
